title: Rehat words
hookLine: writings on Sikh conduct are attributed to Nand Lal; historians discuss when they were set down

cards: A love poet's name, on rules? Nand Lal's name turns up on short writings about how a Sikh should live. Not love songs.

Rules. What to do, what not to do, what a Sikh of the Guru keeps. It's a sudden change of tone, from the beloved's face to the kitchen table of daily life, and it comes with a puzzle about where those writings came from.

teach.b: Rehat is the Sikh word for a way of living: conduct, discipline, the shape of a life. Writings that set it out are called rahitnamas, and some of them carry Nand Lal's name.
One is often called the Tankhahnama, and another is a set of questions and answers.

teach.h: NAND LAL ASKS, THE GURU ANSWERS.
teach.b: They're framed as a conversation: Nand Lal asks, and Guru Gobind Singh answers. What does a Sikh of the Guru do? What should a Sikh avoid?

What's the fault, and how is it put right? The answers are practical. They speak of things like joining the sangat, remembering the Name, honest dealing, and how a Sikh behaves toward the Guru's word and toward others.
Now the puzzle, and here the honest thing is to say it plainly. These writings are attributed to Nand Lal.
Historians discuss when they were actually set down, and whether everything in them comes from his own hand, or was written or added later and given his name.
Sikh scholars and historians don't all read the evidence the same way. That's not a scandal.
It's what can happen to old writing that people treasure: it's copied, recited and handed down, and the question of who wrote which line gets complicated.
Today, Sikhs keep an agreed code of conduct, the Sikh Rehat Maryada, and it's its own document. The rahitnamas are part of the long conversation behind it.
Whatever the dates, the same name that signs love songs to God is attached to rules about daily life: longing for the Beloved, and a discipline kept day by day, side by side.

how: The Sikh Rehat Maryada is the code of conduct agreed by the Panth today, and the older rahitnamas, including those attributed to Nand Lal, are studied as part of its background.

games.q: you've written love songs to God all your life. someone asks: what does a Sikh actually do every day?
o: say love is enough, and rules don't matter.
ask the Guru, and set down the answers about conduct.
games.why: the rahitnamas carrying Nand Lal's name are framed just this way: Nand Lal asks, and the Guru answers about how a Sikh should live.

practice: Find one small rule that would make your days more like the life you want, no phone at the table, a kind word before a hard one, ten minutes of quiet before work, and say it to yourself in one plain sentence.
Picture keeping it at the moment it'll be hardest, and if you pray, you can hold that rule up as a small offering.
